extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, educators, and beginning reporters/editors
extracted.subtask_description: Apply established journalism models (Galtung & Ruge; Shoemaker et al.) to judge which events or story pitches deserve coverage based on factors like timeliness, proximity, impact, prominence, novelty, and editorial composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance of news story to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: West Coast audiences find California earthquakes more newsworthy than distant events. (Listed in Galtung & Ruge model as taught.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (Galtung & Ruge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recency; recent or developing events dominate the modern news cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that have occurred recently or are currently developing are prioritized for coverage. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are easy to understand receive more coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that can be quickly and simply communicated is more likely to be selected by editors. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scheduled events (elections, sports) gain news value as they approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events with known timing accumulate news value leading up to them because they are expected and can be planned for. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpredictable disasters, accidents, or crimes carry significant news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising or unforeseen incidents attract coverage due to their novelty and shock value. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ongoing situations (wars, protests) warrant extended coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that develop over time are kept on the agenda because they provide follow-up opportunities and sustained audience interest. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors balance story selection for variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial judgement includes composing a mix of stories to provide a balanced news agenda rather than focusing on a single type of event. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite People
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians, entertainers, athletes get more coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social status or fame of those involved increases a story's news value; prominent figures attract audience attention. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite Countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Disasters in wealthy/developed nations get more attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geopolitical and economic status of locations affects coverage decisions—events in elite countries are deemed more newsworthy. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news deemed more newsworthy than good news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative events (conflict, disaster, scandal) are more likely to be selected and emphasized than positive developments. (Galtung & Ruge model.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (Shoemaker et al.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like Galtung & Ruge, Shoemaker et al. emphasize recency as a central determinant of whether a story is chosen for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events nearer to the audience's location are considered more relevant and thus more likely to be covered. (Shoemaker et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / Impact / Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: How many people the event affects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that affect large numbers of people or have significant consequences are prioritized for coverage. (Shoemaker et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives that evoke emotion, curiosity, or personal connection increase a story's attractiveness to audiences and editors. (Shoemaker et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict or Controversy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disagreements, disputes, and controversies generate drama and attention, making them more likely to be covered. (Shoemaker et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerated, shocking, or lurid elements can elevate a story's placement and prominence despite potential costs to nuance. (Shoemaker et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The status or fame of the individuals involved increases news value; prominent people attract coverage. (Shoemaker et al.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Oddity / Unusual
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncommon, quirky, or novel events draw curiosity and are more likely to be reported. (Shoemaker et al.)
